analytical_models.model_note: f_gamma = A × e^(-Bε); f_gamma = 19.6·e^(-3.8·ε) for M2-IA. Lower B indicates higher mechanical stability and slower TRIP.

parameters.name: A (austenite fraction before tensile test, M2-IA)

computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Fitting parameter B = 3.8 for M2-IA; measured austenite fractions before (19 %) and after (3.2 %) tensile testing used to fit the model.

defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: After tensile testing, M2-IA exhibits strain partitioning into two distinct regions: a low-KAM region indicating lower strain, most likely in δ-ferrite regions, and a high-KAM region indicating transformed martensite (Fig. 11f/h).

interfaces.interface_notes: Mn concentration profile across the moving α/γ interface during IA at 700 °C: at t=0 flat profiles C_Mn^γ and C_Mn^α/δ; at t=t1 gradients develop between interface and far-field; at t=∞ flat equilibrium steps C_Mn^γ(eq) and C_Mn^α/δ(eq). Mn (and C) partition from ferrite into austenite, Si partitions from austenite to δ-ferrite and α-ferrite (Fig. 9, Fig. 8c).
interfaces.phase_evolution: On heating M2-HR (α-ferrite + martensitic-austenitic α′+γ + δ-ferrite) to the IAT, unstable martensite first transforms to austenite, then the two types of ferrite may also transform to approach the equilibrium ~30 % austenite; the observed austenite fraction (~19 %) is lower than the equilibrium prediction.
interfaces.slip_behavior: Finer austenite grains (γf) with higher Mn and C undergo dislocation glide followed by TRIP at higher strain; coarser grains (γc) transform to martensite earlier (Fig. 12).

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: PSE (product of strength and elongation) and retained austenite fraction: M2-IA PSE = 41 GPa% and 19 % retained austenite vs M1-IA PSE = 61 GPa% and 45 % retained austenite

processing_steps.method: vacuum arc melting followed by 4× remelting
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: The two steel compositions (M1 and M2) were fabricated using a vacuum arc melting furnace. The melted ingot was remelted 4 times by flipping the ingot before each remelt to ensure complete and uniform melting of the raw materials.
Homogenization of as-cast samples was carried out at 1100 °C for 2 h, followed by water quenching (M2-HQ).
Samples were hot-rolled at 1100 °C to reduce the thickness by 50 %, followed by air cooling (M2-HR). Table 1 lists ~50 % thickness reduction at 1100-900 °C.
Intercritical annealing (IA) was carried out at the selected temperature of 700 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching. IAT of 700 °C corresponds to ~11 % Mn in austenite for both steels (M2-IA).

elongated, banded and blocky regions threading between large ferrite grains (EBSD phase map, Fig. 6b)

structures.overall_structure: Intercritically annealed M2 (Fe-8Mn-3Al-1Si-0.2C) comprises multiple phases similar to the hot-rolled microstructure: α-ferrite and austenite with a negligible amount of martensite; in addition a coarse band-type morphology of δ-ferrite is present due to Si addition.

Local microstructural heterogeneity in M2-IA arises from elemental partitioning during IA: Mn and C partition from α/δ-ferrite into austenite while Si partitions from austenite into both δ-ferrite and α-ferrite, raising austenite stability above the equilibrium-composition expectation.

unmapped_findings: PSE (product of strength and elongation) for M2-IA is 41 GPa%, compared to 61 GPa% for the Si-free M1-IA; the higher PSE of M1 is attributed to its higher retained austenite fraction and finer grains resulting in slower TRIP (b0006, b0061, b0076, b0083).

The stacking fault energy (SFE) of both steels is below 18 mJ/m^2, a critical value below which the alloys are expected to show a TRIP effect; transformation of austenite to martensite is expected during deformation (b0061).
The retained austenite fraction in M2-IA decreases from 19 % before the tensile test to 3.2 % after fracture, demonstrating the occurrence of the TRIP effect during deformation (b0067, figure_011).

Despite a lower retained austenite fraction, the presence of δ-ferrite in M2 enhances partitioning of Mn and C into austenite at IAT, making austenite more stable; as a result both steels possess a favourable combination of strength and ductility (b0073).

The calculated retained austenite fraction at RT for M2-IA (~11 %, from Ms + Koistinen-Marburger model) is lower than the observed fraction (~19 %); this discrepancy is attributed to local microstructural heterogeneities: preferential segregation of elements (Mn from α-ferrite and δ-ferrite to austenite, Si from austenite to δ-ferrite) and a high fraction of finer grains raising austenite stability above the equilibrium-composition expectation (b0055).

The fraction of finer grains is relatively lower for M2-IA than M1-IA, so the extent of austenite stability would be lower in M2-IA; this explains the relatively smaller difference between observed and calculated austenite fractions for M2-IA compared to M1-IA (b0055).
M2-IA exhibits a ductile dimple-rupture fracture; austenite present absorbs strain energy during deformation by transforming into martensite, forming fine dimples (b0066, figure_010).
